sections.heading: What is it?
sections.content: Hiragana is one of the three Japanese writing systems. They represent sounds (syllables) and are used for native Japanese words.

sections.heading: Structure
sections.content: 46 basic characters organized in rows by consonant (k, s, t, n, h, m, y, r, w) and columns by vowel (a, i, u, e, o).

sections.heading: Tips
sections.content:
• Start with the vowels (あいうえお)
• Learn one row at a time
• Practice handwriting
• Associate each sound with a mnemonic image

sections.heading: Example
sections.content:
あ (a) looks like a person saying "Ah!"
き (ki) looks like a key

sections.heading: Usage
sections.content:
Katakana is used for:
• Foreign words (コーヒー = coffee)
• Foreign proper names
• Onomatopoeia
• Emphasis (like italics)

sections.heading: Difference with Hiragana
sections.content: Same sounds, more angular shapes. If hiragana = cursive, katakana = block letters.

sections.heading: Tips
sections.content:
• Learn them AFTER hiragana
• Associate each katakana with its hiragana equivalent
• Practice with common words: テレビ (TV), パン (bread)

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.content: The dakuten (゛) or "ten-ten" is a diacritical mark that transforms certain sounds into voiced versions. It's placed at the top right of the character.

sections.heading: Transformations
sections.content:
• K → G (か→が ka→ga)
• S → Z (さ→ざ sa→za)
• T → D (た→だ ta→da)
• H → B (は→ば ha→ba)

Note: し becomes じ (shi→ji) and つ becomes づ (tsu→zu)

sections.heading: Pronunciation
sections.content:
Voiced sounds are pronounced with vocal cord vibration:
• GA, GI, GU, GE, GO (like in 'go')
• ZA, JI, ZU, ZE, ZO (like in 'zoo')
• DA, DI, DU, DE, DO (like in 'do')
• BA, BI, BU, BE, BO (like in 'ball')

sections.heading: Tip
sections.content: First pronounce the base sound (ka, sa, ta, ha) then add 'voice': it's like going from a whisper to normal voice!

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.content: The handakuten (゜) or "maru" (circle) transforms only the H row into P sounds. It's a small circle placed at the top right of the character.

sections.heading: Transformation H → P
sections.content:
• は → ぱ (ha → pa)
• ひ → ぴ (hi → pi)
• ふ → ぷ (hu → pu)
• へ → ぺ (he → pe)
• ほ → ぽ (ho → po)

sections.heading: Pronunciation
sections.content:
The P sound is explosive, like in English:
• PA as in 'papa'
• PI as in 'pizza'
• PU as in 'pull'
• PE as in 'pet'
• PO as in 'pot'

sections.heading: Difference
sections.content:
Don't confuse:
• Dakuten (゛) = H → B (vibration)
• Handakuten (゜) = H → P (air burst)

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.content: Yōon are combinations of two characters forming a single sound. The 2nd character (や, ゆ, よ) is written smaller.

sections.heading: Structure
sections.content:
Consonant + i + small ya/yu/yo:
• きゃ = kya (ki + ya)
• しゅ = shu (shi + yu)
• ちょ = cho (chi + yo)
• りゃ = rya (ri + ya)

sections.heading: Pronunciation
sections.content:
Both characters are pronounced as ONE sound:
• KYA (like 'Kya!' when screaming)
• SHU (like 'shoe')
• CHO (like 'cho' in chocolate)
• NYA (like a cat's meow)

sections.heading: Common usage
sections.content:
Very frequent in Japanese:
• きゃく (kyaku) = guest/customer
• しゅう (shuu) = week
• ちょっと (chotto) = a little
• りょう (ryou) = dormitory

sections.heading: What is it?
sections.content: Characters of Chinese origin representing concepts. Each kanji usually has multiple readings (on'yomi and kun'yomi).

sections.heading: Readings
sections.content:
• On'yomi (音読み): Sino-Japanese reading, used in compound words
• Kun'yomi (訓読み): Native Japanese reading, often standalone

sections.heading: JLPT N5
sections.content: For JLPT N5, you need to know ~100 basic kanji: numbers, days, directions, people, etc.

sections.heading: Method
sections.content:
• Learn the meaning first
• Then the common readings
• Practice with real words
• Use mnemonics!

sections.heading: Approach
sections.content: Learn vocabulary in context, not in isolation. Words stick better with example sentences.

sections.heading: Available themes
sections.content:
• Greetings and politeness (こんにちは, ありがとう...)
• Days of the week (月曜日, 火曜日...)
• Colors (赤, 青, 白...)
• Family (お父さん, お母さん...)
• Basic food (水, ご飯, パン...)

sections.heading: Tips
sections.content:
• Review regularly with SRS
• Listen to pronunciation (audio button)
• Use words in sentences
• Learn 5-10 new words per day maximum

sections.heading: JLPT N5 Vocabulary
sections.content: These lessons cover essential vocabulary for JLPT N5 (beginner level). About 800 words to master for the test.

sections.heading: System
sections.content:
Japanese uses two systems:
• Sino-Japanese: いち、に、さん...
• Native Japanese: ひとつ、ふたつ...

sections.heading: Counters
sections.content:
Japanese uses 'counters' depending on the object:
• 人 (nin) for people
• 本 (hon) for long objects
• 枚 (mai) for flat objects

sections.heading: Irregularities
sections.content:
Watch out for phonetic changes:
• 1人 = ひとり (not いちにん)
• 2人 = ふたり
• 4 = よん or し
• 7 = なな or しち

sections.heading: Consistency
sections.content: 15 minutes a day is better than 2 hours once a week. Regularity is key!

sections.heading: Spaced repetition
sections.content: Use the SRS (Spaced Repetition System) to review at the optimal moment and retain knowledge long-term.

sections.heading: Immersion
sections.content:
• Listen to Japanese (anime, music, podcasts)
• Change your phone language
• Label objects in your home
